title: Git and GitHub
readingMarkdown:
# Git and GitHub

**Git** records the history of a project as a series of snapshots, lets several lines of work proceed in parallel, and lets you return to any earlier state. **GitHub** hosts Git repositories online and adds collaboration: pull requests, reviews, issues, and automation. For AI-assisted development, Git is not optional: it is the **safety net** that turns an agent's bad afternoon into a one-command rollback, the record that lets you bisect a bug to a single change, Module 9.9, and the review gate between what an AI wrote and what reaches users.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### A photo album of the project, with sticky notes

Imagine photographing your whole workshop every time you finish a piece of work, writing on the back what you did and why, and keeping the photos in order. That album is the **commit history**. A **branch** is a sticky note marking which photo you are currently building on; making a new branch is just adding another sticky note, so you can try something without disturbing the main line. **Merging** combines the work of two branches into a new photo. A **remote**, such as GitHub, is a copy of the album kept somewhere else, shared with your team.

```text
   main:     A --- B --- C --- D                    each letter is a commit: a snapshot + parent(s) + message
                    \
   feature:          E --- F                        branch = a movable pointer to a commit
                                                    merge F into D: merge base B, three-way merge -> M
   main:     A --- B --- C --- D --- M
                    \               /
                     E ----------- F

   GITHUB FLOW
   issue #42 -> branch fix/bundle-price -> small commits -> push -> pull request
      -> CI checks + review (approve / request changes) -> merge to protected main -> deploy (Module 9.11)
```

### Why Git matters more with AI

An agent can change twenty files in a minute. Without version control, a bad change is a disaster: you cannot easily see what changed or put it back. With Git, every change is a diff you can read, every state is a commit you can return to, and every branch is a sandbox. The habits this module teaches, small commits, branches per task, review before merge, are what make it safe to let an AI work fast.

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### Commits are content-addressed

A commit records a **snapshot** of the files, a pointer to its **parent** commit or commits, the author, and a **message**. Git identifies each commit by a hash of its content, a SHA-1 hash by default, so the identifier is a fingerprint: change one byte of the snapshot, the parent, or the message, and the identifier changes. Two consequences matter. History is **tamper-evident**, the same idea as Module 8.14's hash-chained audit log, because each commit includes its parent's identifier. And identical content always gets the identical identifier. The lab hashes a simplified commit text; real Git also prefixes a header with the object type and length.

### Branches, merges, and the merge base

A branch is a lightweight, movable name for a commit. When two branches have diverged, Git combines them using their **merge base**, the best common ancestor, which `git merge-base` reports. Three situations arise:

| Situation | What Git does |
|---|---|
| The other branch is already in your history | Nothing: already up to date |
| Your branch is an ancestor of the other | **Fast-forward**: move your pointer forward, no new commit |
| Both have new commits since the base | **Three-way merge**: combine changes relative to the base, creating a merge commit |

### Three-way merge and conflicts

A three-way merge compares each region of the file in three versions: the **base**, **ours**, and **theirs**. For each region:

| Base vs ours | Base vs theirs | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Same | Same | Base |
| Changed | Same | Ours |
| Same | Changed | Theirs |
| Changed | Changed, same change | That change |
| Changed | Changed, different changes | **Conflict** |

A conflict is not an error; it is Git refusing to guess when both sides changed the same lines differently. It marks the region with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` and asks a person to decide. AI tools can propose resolutions, but the resolution is a decision about intent, so read it. Two agents working in parallel on the same file produce conflicts constantly, one reason Module 8.9 warns against splitting coupled work.

### Remotes

A **remote** is another copy of the repository, usually on GitHub. `git push` sends your commits to it; `git pull` fetches others' commits and merges them into yours. A remote is also your **backup**: commits that exist only on a laptop are lost with the laptop.

### The GitHub flow

GitHub's documentation describes a lightweight, branch-based workflow, the **GitHub flow**: create a branch for each change, make commits on it, open a **pull request**, discuss and review, address feedback, merge into the main branch, and delete the branch. Pull requests tie together the description of the change, a linked **issue** describing the problem, the diff, automated checks, and **reviews**, in which reviewers can comment, approve, or request changes.

**Protected branches** let repository owners enforce rules on the main branch, such as requiring pull requests, passing status checks, approving reviews, and an up-to-date branch before merging. For AI-assisted teams these rules are the guardrails of Module 9.2 implemented in the hosting platform: no agent, and no person, pushes straight to main.

### Small changes

Google's engineering practices recommend small changes, "small CLs", because they are reviewed more quickly and more thoroughly, are less likely to introduce bugs, are easier to roll back, and are easier to merge. A common rule of thumb in teams is that a pull request of a few hundred changed lines is reviewable and a few thousand is not. Size also makes bisection effective. AI agents naturally produce large diffs; asking for one task per branch, and splitting large changes into a sequence of small pull requests, keeps review real.

### Commit messages

A commit message is a note to your future self and colleagues about **why** a change was made. Chris Beams's widely cited guide recommends a concise subject line, around 50 characters with a hard limit near 72, written in the imperative mood ("Fix bundle price lookup"), without a trailing full stop, followed by a blank line and a body explaining what and why. Vague messages such as "fix stuff" defeat the purpose of history; AI tools can draft good messages from a diff, but check that the "why" is right.

### Git as a safety net for AI changes

| Habit | Protects against |
|---|---|
| Commit before letting an agent loose | Losing the last good state |
| A branch per task | Experiments leaking into main |
| Commit after each working step | Large rollbacks, Module 9.2 |
| Read `git diff` before every commit | Unreviewed deletions, secrets, out-of-scope edits, Module 9.1 |
| `.gitignore` for `.env` and keys | Secrets entering history permanently |
| Pull requests with CI and review | Broken or unreviewed code reaching main |
| `git revert` for shared history | Undoing a merged change safely, with a record |

Secrets deserve special mention: once a key is committed and pushed, assume it is compromised, even if a later commit removes it, because the history still contains it. Rotate the key.

### Complexity

Hashing a commit is linear in its content. Walking ancestors is roughly linear in history. The simplified line-by-line three-way merge is linear in lines; real merges first align lines with a diff algorithm. Pull request and commit checks are constant or linear in files.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

First, content-addressed commit identifiers.

```python
import hashlib

def commit_id(tree, parents, message):
    content = f"tree {tree}\n" + "".join(f"parent {p}\n" for p in parents) + f"\n{message}\n"
    return hashlib.sha1(content.encode()).hexdigest()[:7]

print(commit_id("4b825dc", [], "Initial commit"))
print(commit_id("4b825dc", [], "Initial commit"))
print(commit_id("4b825dc", [], "Initial commit!"))
```

- **The identifier is a hash of the snapshot, the parents, and the message.**
- **The same content gives the same identifier, every time.**
- **One extra character changes it completely.** Because each commit includes its parents' identifiers, rewriting any old commit changes every later one.

Next, deciding the kind of merge.

```python
def ancestors(commits, cid):
    seen, stack = [], [cid]
    while stack:
        c = stack.pop()
        if c not in seen:
            seen.append(c)
            stack.extend(commits[c])
    return seen

def merge_kind(commits, ours, theirs):
    mine, other = ancestors(commits, ours), ancestors(commits, theirs)
    if theirs in mine:
        return "already up to date", theirs
    if ours in other:
        return "fast-forward", ours
    return "three-way merge", next(c for c in mine if c in other)

GRAPH = {"A": [], "B": ["A"], "C": ["B"], "D": ["C"], "E": ["B"], "F": ["E"]}
print(merge_kind(GRAPH, "D", "F"), merge_kind(GRAPH, "C", "D"), merge_kind(GRAPH, "D", "B"))
```

- **The graph maps each commit to its parents.** Main is A, B, C, D; the feature branch left at B with E and F.
- **Merging F into D needs a three-way merge with base B.** Both sides moved on since B.
- **Merging D into C is a fast-forward.** C is behind D on the same line.
- **Merging B into D does nothing.** B is already in D's history.
- **The lab's merge base is the first common ancestor found from our side.** Exact for these histories; Git's algorithm handles more complex graphs.

Then, a line-level three-way merge.

```python
def three_way(base, ours, theirs):
    merged, conflicts = [], 0
    for b, o, t in zip(base, ours, theirs):
        if o == t:
            merged.append(o)
        elif o == b:
            merged.append(t)
        elif t == b:
            merged.append(o)
        else:
            conflicts += 1
            merged += ["<<<<<<< ours", o, "=======", t, ">>>>>>> theirs"]
    return merged, conflicts

BASE = ["price = 89", "discount = 0", "tax = 0.2"]
print(three_way(BASE, ["price = 89", "discount = 0.1", "tax = 0.2"], ["price = 79", "discount = 0", "tax = 0.2"]))
print(three_way(BASE, ["price = 89", "discount = 0.1", "tax = 0.2"], ["price = 89", "discount = 0.15", "tax = 0.2"]))
```

- **We changed the discount; they changed the price.** Different lines, so both changes are kept, no conflict.
- **When both change the discount differently, the region is a conflict with markers.** Git will not guess whether 0.1 or 0.15 is right.
- **The lab assumes the three versions have the same number of lines.** Real merges align lines first.

Then, pull request checks.

```python
def pr_blockers(pr, max_lines=400):
    blockers = []
    if not pr["description"].strip():
        blockers.append("no description")
    if not pr["linked_issue"]:
        blockers.append("no linked issue")
    if pr["ci"] != "success":
        blockers.append(f"CI {pr['ci']}")
    if pr["approvals"] < 1:
        blockers.append("needs an approving review")
    if pr["changes_requested"]:
        blockers.append("changes requested")
    if pr["behind_main"]:
        blockers.append("branch is behind main")
    size = pr["additions"] + pr["deletions"]
    if size > max_lines:
        blockers.append(f"{size} lines changed; split it")
    return ("ready to merge" if not blockers else "blocked"), blockers

PR = {"description": "Fix bundle pricing for BLADE-10, closes issue 42", "linked_issue": 42, "ci": "success", "approvals": 1,
      "changes_requested": False, "behind_main": False, "additions": 38, "deletions": 6}
print(pr_blockers(PR))
print(pr_blockers({**PR, "description": "", "ci": "failure", "approvals": 0, "additions": 1900, "behind_main": True}))
```

- **A small, described, linked, reviewed pull request with green checks is ready.**
- **The AI-generated mega-change fails five rules at once.** No description, failing CI, no review, out of date, and 1,906 lines.
- **Protected-branch rules enforce the same checks on GitHub itself.** The function is the team's policy written down.

Finally, commit hygiene.

```python
GENERIC = {"update", "fix", "changes", "wip", "stuff", "misc", "fix stuff", "updates"}
SENSITIVE = (".pem", "id_rsa", "credentials.json")

def commit_check(message, files, max_files=10):
    issues = []
    lines = message.strip().splitlines()
    summary = lines[0] if lines else ""
    if not summary:
        issues.append("empty message")
    elif summary.lower().rstrip(".") in GENERIC:
        issues.append("summary too vague")
    if len(summary) > 72:
        issues.append(f"summary is {len(summary)} characters")
    if summary.endswith("."):
        issues.append("summary ends with a full stop")
    leaked = [f for f in files if f.rsplit("/", 1)[-1].startswith(".env") or f.endswith(SENSITIVE)]
    if leaked:
        issues.append(f"sensitive files staged: {', '.join(leaked)}")
    if len(files) > max_files:
        issues.append(f"{len(files)} files; one task per commit")
    return not issues, issues

print(commit_check("Fix bundle price lookup for BLADE-10\n\nThe bundle table removed the item from the price index.",
                   ["app/pricing.py", "tests/test_pricing.py"]))
print(commit_check("fix stuff", [".env", "app/pricing.py"] + [f"app/m{i}.py" for i in range(12)]))
```

- **A specific imperative summary with a body explaining why passes.**
- **"fix stuff" tells nobody anything.**
- **A staged `.env` file is caught before it enters history.** Once pushed, the only safe response is rotating every key in it.
- **Fourteen files suggests several tasks in one commit.** Split it, so bisection and rollback stay precise.

**Complexity.** `commit_id` is linear in the content. `ancestors` and `merge_kind` are roughly linear in history; the list-based seen check makes them quadratic in the worst case. `three_way` is linear in lines. `pr_blockers` is constant. `commit_check` is linear in files.

### A repository setup for AI-assisted work

```text
MAIN BRANCH    protected: pull requests required; CI must pass; 1 approving review; up to date; no force pushes
BRANCHES       one per task: fix/bundle-price, feat/csv-export; deleted after merge
COMMITS        after each working step; imperative summary <= 72 chars; body says why; one task each
AGENTS         start from a clean commit; work on a branch; never push to main; diff reviewed before commit
.gitignore     .env*, *.pem, credentials.json, node_modules/, build output
PULL REQUESTS  description + linked issue; under ~400 changed lines; CI tests and lint
UNDO           local experiments: git reset or git restore; shared history: git revert
SECRETS        committed by mistake -> rotate immediately, then clean history if required
```

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**No commit before the agent starts.** Without a clean starting point, there is nothing to return to. Commit first.

**Working on main.** Experiments land in the shared line. Branch for every task.

**Giant commits.** "Agent session, all changes" cannot be reviewed or bisected. Commit each working step.

**Committing without reading the diff.** Deleted tests and pasted secrets slip in. Read `git diff --staged` every time.

**Secrets in history.** Deleting the file in a later commit leaves it in history. Rotate the secret.

**Rewriting shared history.** Force-pushing over teammates' work loses it. Use `git revert` on shared branches; protect main.

**Resolving conflicts by accepting one side blindly.** Both sides usually had a reason. Read the markers and the intent.

**Long-lived branches.** The longer a branch lives, the worse its conflicts. Merge small and often.

**Pull requests without context.** "Updates" with 40 files wastes reviewers' time. Describe what, why, and how to test.

**Approving AI pull requests on trust.** The review is the last human check. Review as carefully as a colleague's code.

**Vague messages.** "fix" will not help anyone in six months. Say what and why.

**Laptop-only repositories.** A dead disk loses everything. Push to a remote.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** Git records a project as content-addressed commits, each a snapshot with parents and a message identified by a hash, making history tamper-evident; branches are movable names for commits, and remotes such as GitHub hold shared copies and backups. Merging two branches is a no-op if one already contains the other, a fast-forward if ours is an ancestor of theirs, and otherwise a three-way merge against their merge base, where changes on different lines combine and different changes to the same lines become conflicts for a person to resolve. The GitHub flow runs from a branch per change through commits, a pull request with a description and linked issue, automated checks, review, and merge into a protected main branch that enforces those rules. Small changes are reviewed better and roll back cleaner, commit messages should say what and why in an imperative summary of at most about 72 characters, and secrets must never be committed, or must be rotated if they are. For AI-assisted work, Git is the safety net: commit before and during agent work, branch per task, read every diff, and merge only reviewed, passing pull requests.

**Question 1.** An agent worked for an hour directly on `main`, committing once at the end with the message "agent changes" across 34 files, and checkout is now broken. Explain what this makes hard, using the module's tools, and describe the workflow that would have made it easy.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

`commit_check` on that commit reports 34 files, more than one task per commit; the summary "agent changes" slips past the lab's short list of generic phrases, but it says nothing about what changed or why. With a single large commit, there are only two states, before and after, so `git bisect` from Module 9.9 can only point at the whole hour of work, and reverting it throws away everything, good and bad, together. Because the work is on main, anyone who pulled since has the broken code, and reverting rewrites shared state, so it must be done with `git revert`, which adds an inverse commit, rather than by resetting history. The fix is to read the 34-file diff to find the checkout change, or revert the whole commit and redo the good parts. The workflow that makes it easy: commit the clean state first; create a branch such as `feat/bundles`; let the agent work there, committing after each working step with a specific message, so bisection lands on a small change; read the diff before each commit; open a pull request into a protected main branch that requires passing CI and an approving review, so the broken checkout would have failed CI before merging; and keep each pull request under a few hundred lines.

</details>

**Question 2.** Two developers branched from commit B. One changed the discount line, the other the price line, and later both changed the discount line to different values. Use `merge_kind` and `three_way` to explain what Git does in each case.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

In the module's graph, main moved from B to C and D while the feature branch moved from B to E and F, so `merge_kind(GRAPH, "D", "F")` reports a three-way merge with merge base B: neither branch contains the other, and both have new commits since B. Git compares each region with the base. In the first case, ours changed the discount from 0 to 0.1 and theirs changed the price from 89 to 79; for each line only one side differs from the base, so `three_way` takes that side's version and produces price 79 and discount 0.1 with no conflicts: both developers' work is kept automatically. In the second case, both sides changed the discount line from the base, one to 0.1 and one to 0.15; `three_way` cannot know which is intended, so it emits conflict markers around the two versions and counts one conflict. A person must decide, perhaps by asking both developers or checking the issue, and then edit the file to the intended value, remove the markers, and commit the merge. An AI can suggest a resolution, but it is a decision about intent, not syntax, so it must be checked.

</details>

**Question 3.** A developer accidentally committed and pushed `.env` with live payment and email keys, then deleted the file in the next commit. Explain why that is not enough, and what to do, including how `commit_check` and the repository setup prevent a repeat.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

Git history keeps every snapshot: the commit that added `.env` still contains the keys, and anyone with access to the repository, or to any clone or fork made since the push, can read them by checking out that commit. Deleting the file in a later commit only removes it from the latest snapshot. Because the repository was pushed, the keys must be treated as compromised. The response, in order: rotate the payment and email keys immediately at the providers, revoking the old ones; check the providers' logs for use of the old keys; then, if policy requires, rewrite the history to remove the file, with a history-cleaning tool and a coordinated force push, accepting that existing clones still hold the old history, which is why rotation comes first. To prevent a repeat, add `.env*` and other secret files to `.gitignore`; run a check like `commit_check`, which flags `sensitive files staged: .env` before the commit is made, as a pre-commit hook; enable secret scanning on the hosting platform; keep secrets in environment variables or a secrets manager, Module 9.11; and make reading `git diff --staged` part of every commit, especially after an agent session.

</details>

steps.instruction: Implement merge_kind(commits, ours, theirs) using ancestors. If theirs is among our ancestors, return ('already up to date', theirs). Classify five merges, in both directions and from the root. This is branches, merges, and the merge base from Section 2. [MOD-9.10]
steps.hintConceptual: If their photos are already in your album, nothing to do; if your album is just an earlier part of theirs, skip ahead; otherwise find the last photo you both share and combine from there.

steps.title: Merge three ways
steps.instruction: Implement three_way(base, ours, theirs). For each line triple: if ours equals theirs keep it; else if ours equals the base take theirs; else if theirs equals the base take ours; otherwise count a conflict and add '<<<<<<< ours', our line, '=======', their line, and '>>>>>>> theirs'. Return the merged lines and the conflict count. Merge changes to different lines, conflicting changes to the same line, an identical change on both sides, and no change. This is three-way merge and conflicts from Section 2. [MOD-9.10]
steps.hintConceptual: For each line, see who changed it since the shared original: keep the one change if only one person changed it, and if both changed it differently, put both on the table for a person to choose.

assert _n == 1 and _m == ["price = 89", "<<<<<<< ours", "discount = 0.1", "=======", "discount = 0.15", ">>>>>>> theirs", "tax = 0.2"], f"A conflict, got {_m}"
assert three_way(BASE, ["price = 99"] + BASE[1:], ["price = 99"] + BASE[1:]) == (["price = 99"] + BASE[1:], 0), "The same change on both sides"
assert three_way(BASE, BASE, BASE) == (BASE, 0), "Nothing changed"
print("Step 3 passed: price and discount changes combine; two different discounts conflict.")

steps.title: Check a pull request
steps.instruction: Implement pr_blockers(pr, max_lines). Collect, in order: 'no description' if the description is blank; 'no linked issue'; 'CI <status>' unless CI is 'success'; 'needs an approving review' with no approvals; 'changes requested'; 'branch is behind main'; '<additions + deletions> lines changed; split it' when above max_lines. Return ('ready to merge', []) or ('blocked', blockers). Check a good pull request, an AI-generated mega-change, one with no linked issue, pending CI, and requested changes, and the 400-line boundary. This is the GitHub flow and small changes from Section 2. [MOD-9.10]
steps.hintConceptual: Before the change joins the main album, check it has a caption, a reason, passing checks, a reviewer's nod, is up to date, and is small enough for anyone to actually review.
steps.testAssertion:
assert pr_blockers(PR) == ("ready to merge", []), f"A good pull request, got {pr_blockers(PR)}"
assert pr_blockers({**PR, "description": "", "ci": "failure", "approvals": 0, "additions": 1900, "behind_main": True}) == ("blocked", ["no description", "CI failure", "needs an approving review", "branch is behind main", "1906 lines changed; split it"]), "Five blockers"
assert pr_blockers({**PR, "linked_issue": None, "changes_requested": True, "ci": "pending"})[1] == ["no linked issue", "CI pending", "changes requested"], "Issue, pending CI, requested changes"
assert pr_blockers({**PR, "additions": 394})[0] == "ready to merge" and pr_blockers({**PR, "additions": 395})[1] == ["401 lines changed; split it"], "The size boundary"
print("Step 4 passed: the 1,906-line AI change is blocked five ways.")

steps.title: Vet a commit
steps.instruction: Implement commit_check(message, files, max_files). The summary is the first line of the stripped message. Collect: 'empty message' if there is no summary, otherwise 'summary too vague' if its lower-cased form without a trailing full stop is in GENERIC; 'summary is <n> characters' if longer than 72; 'summary ends with a full stop'; 'sensitive files staged: <files joined by ", ">' for files whose name starts with '.env' or that end with an entry in SENSITIVE; '<n> files; one task per commit' if more than max_files. Return whether there are no issues, and the issues. Vet a good commit, a bad commit, empty and vague messages, and a long summary with nested secret files. This is commit messages and Git as a safety net from Section 2. [MOD-9.10]
steps.hintConceptual: Every note on the back of a photo should say clearly what changed and why, the photo should show one job, and nothing private should be in the frame.
steps.testAssertion:
assert commit_check("Fix bundle price lookup for BLADE-10\n\nThe bundle table removed the item from the price index.", ["app/pricing.py", "tests/test_pricing.py"]) == (True, []), "A good commit"
assert commit_check("fix stuff", [".env", "app/pricing.py"] + [f"app/m{i}.py" for i in range(12)]) == (False, ["summary too vague", "sensitive files staged: .env", "14 files; one task per commit"]), f"A bad commit, got {commit_check('fix stuff', ['.env'])}"
assert commit_check("", ["a.py"]) == (False, ["empty message"]) and commit_check("Update.", ["a.py"])[1] == ["summary too vague", "summary ends with a full stop"], "Empty and vague"
assert commit_check("x" * 80, ["config/.env.local", "keys/server.pem"])[1] == ["summary is 80 characters", "sensitive files staged: config/.env.local, keys/server.pem"], "Long summary; nested secrets"
print("Step 5 passed: 'fix stuff' with a staged .env and 14 files is stopped before it enters history.")
